title: 6. 10-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet
book_title: Chapter 6: Follow the Cash — Financial Forensics, CHIPS Credits & Balance Sheet

epigraph.quote: Accounting earnings tell you what the fab cost yesterday; free cash flow after capex and working capital tells you what the owners actually get to keep.
epigraph.author: Forensic Accounting Principle

web_blocks.html: Texas Instruments' statements from FY2021 through Q3 2026 show a clear V-shaped capital cycle [1, 2, 7]. Across that span, TI kept its return on invested capital (ROIC) at an elite 22.04% TTM as of Q3 2026 [1, 2]. Return on equity reached 39.50% and return on assets hit 19.69%. TI posted those marks even after spending $14.44 billion on gross capex from 2023 to 2025 [1, 2, 7].

web_blocks.caption: Annual Financial Summary: FY2021–FY2025 ($ Millions, except per-share & days)
web_blocks.takeaway: *FY2025 GAAP pre-tax income ($6,023M op. profit + $230M OI&E - $543M interest = $5,710M) less $709M tax = $5,001M (some aggregators report $4,973M net of participating securities). Between 2023 and 2025, dividends ($14.35B) exceeded FCF ($5.79B), bridged by cash and debt.

web_blocks.caption: 2026 Quarterly Inflection: Q1–Q3 2026 Progression ($ Millions, except EPS & DIO)
web_blocks.takeaway: Q3 2026 marked a decisive financial inflection: revenue hit $6.06B (+28% YoY), operating margin reached 47.5%, and TTM Free Cash Flow surged to $8.42B—more than covering the ~$5.2B annual dividend.

web_blocks.html: Forensic Check 1 — CHIPS Act Accounting & Cash Quality: Analysts must separate core operating cash flow from one-time government grants [1, 2, 5]. TI defines Free Cash Flow as operating cash flow minus capex plus U.S. CHIPS Act proceeds [1, 2]. In FY2025, CFO ($7,153M) included $335M of CHIPS Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) that cut taxes owed, down from $588M in FY2024. Cost of Revenue also got a $353M boost from lower depreciation ($159M in 2024, $45M in 2023) [1]. Over the TTM period ended Q3 2026, TTM FCF of $8,422M included $1.6 billion of CHIPS ITCs and direct grants [2]. Even without that $1.6B boost, ex-CHIPS TTM FCF hit ~$6.82 billion. That easily covers the ~$5.2B annual dividend [2].

Forensic Check 2 — Dividend Coverage & Capital Allocation Bridge: From 2023 to 2025, TI paid $14,351M in dividends and bought back $2,699M of stock. Over that same span, cumulative FCF was just $5,785M [1, 7]. Management filled that ~$11.3B gap by spending cash reserves and issuing fixed-rate notes. Total debt rose to $14,048M by year-end 2025 ($500M current plus $13,548M long-term) [1]. In September 2026, TI hiked its quarterly dividend by 7% to $1.52 per share ($6.08 annualized). That marked its 23rd straight year of dividend increases [9]. Now that TTM FCF has jumped to $8.42B ($6.82B ex-CHIPS), organic cash flow once again funds the payout [2].

Forensic Check 3 — Balance Sheet & Silicon Labs Funding Capacity: At Q3 2026, TI held $8.1 billion in cash and short-term investments against $13.65 billion in total debt [2]. TI repaid $500M of debt in Q3 2026. Its debt carries a low 4.11% average coupon, with a 5.59 current ratio and 4.05 quick ratio [2]. Net debt of $5.55 billion is modest next to ~$9.90B of TTM CFO [2]. Still, the $7.5 billion all-cash Silicon Labs deal (expected H1 2027) will use most of that $8.1B cash pile or require new bonds [6]. Share buybacks will likely stay slow in 2027 and 2028 while TI funds the deal and trims debt.

Forensic Check 4 — Working Capital & Cash Conversion Cycle: Because TI sells >80% direct and holds a deep die bank, its cash cycle runs longer than fabless peers [1, 4]. Days Sales Outstanding (DSO) stays tight near 38 to 42 days. Inventory days (194 days in Q3 2026, down from 241 days at end-2024) drive most working capital [1, 2]. As sales jumped +28% YoY in Q3 2026, TI did not add inventory dollars. It held inventory flat near $4.7B while shipping more product, which released cash into Q3's $2,956M free cash flow [2].

Forensic Check 5 — Share Count Discipline & Capital Return Sequencing: From 2021 to 2026, TI kept its diluted share count flat near ~914 million shares (914M in 2021, 913M in 2022, 914M in 2023, 920M in 2024, ~914M in 2025–2026) [1, 7]. Stock pay never diluted owners during peak capex years. With the $7.5B Silicon Labs deal closing in H1 2027, buybacks will take a back seat through 2027. Once net debt normalizes, repurchases can resume as a steady FCF-per-share driver [6].

Forensic Check 6 — Earnings Quality & Accruals Verification: Comparing GAAP net income to operating cash flow proves clean earnings quality [1, 7]. From FY2021 to FY2025, GAAP net income totaled $32,697 million ($7,736M + $8,709M + $6,476M + $4,775M + $5,001M). Over those five years, Cash Flow from Operations reached $37,367 million—a 114.3% cash conversion ratio [1, 7]. Even in the 2024 trough, CFO ($6,318M) beat GAAP net income ($4,775M) by $1,543 million as 300mm depreciation ($1,508M) added back to cash [1]. In Q3 2026, CFO ($3,419M implied from $2,956M FCF plus $463M capex) stayed well above net income ($2,425M). That proves TI's 2026 rebound rests on real cash [2].

web_blocks.title: FORENSIC WATCH: EX-CHIPS FCF & DEAL LEVERAGE
paragraphs: Always track TI's FCF both with and without CHIPS Act cash ($1.6B in TTM Q3 2026). Grants and tax credits are real cash, but they end over time. Long-term gains require ex-CHIPS FCF (~$6.8B TTM) to scale past $8B–$9B as capex stays at $2B–$3B and Silicon Labs integrates smoothly.

book_paragraphs: Now let's put on our forensic accountant's visor and follow every dollar of cash through Texas Instruments' statements from 2021 through Q3 2026. If you only glanced at headline Free Cash Flow in 2023 ($1.35 billion) and 2024 ($1.50 billion), you might have wondered how a company paying $4.8 billion a year in dividends could possibly sustain itself.

Here is what actually happened behind the curtain. Between 2023 and 2025, TI paid out $14.35 billion in dividends and bought back $2.70 billion of stock, while cumulative Free Cash Flow was just $5.79 billion. Management deliberately bridged that gap using balance-sheet cash and low-coupon debt—pushing total debt up to $14.05 billion by the end of 2025—because it knew the $14.44 billion capex wave was temporary.

In 2026, the cash-flow bridge snapped back into surplus. Through Q3 2026, trailing-12-month operating cash flow surged to $9.90 billion, capex fell to $2.58 billion, and TTM Free Cash Flow exploded to $8.42 billion. That easily covered the dividend—even after TI's September 2026 7% dividend hike to $1.52 per quarter, its 23rd consecutive annual increase.

Still, a sharp forensic analyst never takes a headline FCF number at face value. That $8.42 billion TTM Free Cash Flow includes $1.6 billion of U.S. CHIPS Act incentives—a mix of direct grants and Investment Tax Credits. Even if you strip out every penny of CHIPS money, underlying ex-CHIPS Free Cash Flow sits around $6.82 billion, which comfortably covers the ~$5.2 billion dividend.

book_subsections.title: The Balance Sheet & the $7.5B Silicon Labs Check
paragraphs: As of Q3 2026, TI sits on $8.1 billion in cash and short-term investments against $13.65 billion in total debt at a very comfortable 4.11% weighted-average coupon, with a 5.59 current ratio. That leaves net debt at just $5.55 billion against nearly $10 billion of annual operating cash flow.

Look closely at the quality of that balance sheet: TI's debt is long-dated, fixed-rate, and staggered across maturities so the company never faces a refinancing cliff. Even during the 2024 trough, interest expense of $508 million was covered more than ten times over by operating profit ($5,350 million) and more than twelve times over by operating cash flow ($6,318 million).

The one major capital-allocation variable ahead is the $7.5 billion all-cash check TI agreed to write for Silicon Labs, expected to close in the first half of 2027. Writing that check will absorb most of the $8.1 billion cash pile or require fresh debt, which likely means share buybacks stay on the back burner until 2028 while cash flow rebuilds the balance sheet.

There is one final forensic check every long-term owner should appreciate: working-capital discipline during an upturn. In Q3 2026, TI's revenue jumped 28% year-over-year to $6.06 billion, yet inventory held roughly flat near $4.7 billion—bringing Days of Inventory down from 241 days at the end of 2024 to 194 days. Because TI did not have to pour cash into restocking its own warehouses while sales surged, operating cash flow converted cleanly into a $2.96 billion single-quarter Free Cash Flow print.

Put the entire ten-year forensic picture together and the quality of the franchise stands out. Return on invested capital sits at 22.04% and return on equity at 39.50%, even after absorbing a $14.44 billion three-year capex wave. Diluted share count has stayed remarkably disciplined around 914 million shares over the last five years, and the dividend has grown for 23 consecutive years. The 2023–2025 cash squeeze was a deliberate capital-allocation choice—not a crack in the underlying economics.

Finally, consider how TI's capital allocation priorities shift from 2027 onward. During 2023–2025, management prioritized 300mm fab construction and the dividend while keeping buybacks modest ($293 million in 2023, $929 million in 2024, $1,477 million in 2025). Once Silicon Labs closes in H1 2027 and gross capex stays disciplined at $2 billion to $3 billion annually, surplus ex-CHIPS free cash flow above the ~$5.2 billion dividend will rebuild cash reserves and gradually restore TI's traditional share-repurchase engine—driving steady per-share compounding across the rest of the decade.

Let us also double-check one accounting detail that often trips up casual readers of semiconductor financial statements: how TI accounts for CHIPS Act Investment Tax Credits and direct grants. On the income statement, the 25% ITC lowers the carrying cost of newly placed-in-service 300mm fab equipment, which reduces annual depreciation inside Cost of Revenue ($353 million reduction in FY2025, up from $159 million in FY2024 and $45 million in FY2023). On the cash flow statement, actual cash tax offsets and grant receipts ($1.6 billion over the trailing twelve months through Q3 2026) boost operating cash flow and non-GAAP Free Cash Flow. Separating that $1.6 billion cash lump from the $6.82 billion of underlying ex-CHIPS FCF ensures we never confuse temporary government subsidies with permanent recurring cash generation.

Equally reassuring is TI's debt maturity ladder and interest coverage. Carrying $13.65 billion of gross debt at a 4.11% weighted-average fixed coupon means annual interest expense sits around $540 million—covered roughly sixteen times over by trailing-12-month operating profit and eighteen times over by operating cash flow. Even after funding the $7.5 billion Silicon Labs acquisition in H1 2027, TI will remain solidly investment-grade with ample liquidity.

Finally, check the earnings-quality ratio across the full five-year cycle from 2021 through 2025. Cumulative GAAP net income totaled $32.70 billion, while cumulative Cash Flow from Operations reached $37.37 billion—a 114.3% cash conversion ratio. Even in the 2024 cyclical trough, operating cash flow ($6.32 billion) exceeded GAAP net income ($4.78 billion) by $1.54 billion, and in Q3 2026 operating cash flow continued to track well ahead of net income. That confirms TI's 2026 rebound is backed by real cash, not accounting accruals.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: The forensic verdict on TI's financials is clean: return on invested capital sits at 22.0%, ROE at 39.5%, debt carries a 4.11% average coupon, and ex-CHIPS free cash flow (~$6.8B TTM) once again covers the dividend with room to spare. The temporary 2023–2025 cash-flow squeeze was capex-driven, not earnings-quality decay.
